passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the church clock strikes seven and the last children leave the schoolyard, and still the birds wheel overhead. Then the streetlights on the hill come on, and the first swifts drop into the chimney, each with a sharp bank to the left, while the last bus passes the school gates.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his totals fill four notebooks. This year's best, 6,140, is the largest roost he has ever recorded. Those notebooks are the reason the chimney is still standing.

The storm two winters ago split the chimney with a crack from its top to the roofline. The council proposed having it pulled down, since a proper repair would cost more than demolition. Reyburn went to the March meeting, he told me, only to ask whether the work could wait until the swifts had left, and he set his notebooks on the table because he had carried them in. The councillors read them through and voted to keep the chimney standing for the swifts.

The masons who mended it chose lime mortar matched to the old, knowing that cheap cement would crack the soft brick and dry too smooth for a swift's claws. A century after it was built, the chimney stands as straight and sound as the day its last brick was laid, the best-made thing on the hill.

Whoever laid that brick built well enough for a furnace and, a hundred years on, well enough for six thousand swifts. In early October the birds will leave for the south, and the chimney will stand over the empty schoolyard until they return in May, as solid as it has always been.

Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge into a bank of cloud, the streetlights on the hill come on, and still the birds wheel overhead. Then the church clock strikes seven, and the first swifts drop into the chimney; the last children leave the schoolyard and the last bus passes the school gates while the rest pour in after them.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. In 1990 he repointed the whole chimney himself with lime and sand, and he can still tell you which courses of its brick are soft. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his notebooks show the roost holding steady at about five thousand birds, as he expects it to next year.

The storm two winters ago split the chimney with a crack from its top to the roofline. The council kept the chimney standing, since having it pulled down would have meant scaffolding the whole roof. Reyburn wrote to the council to warn that cement would crack the old brick, and asked for lime, expecting the councillors to agree. They voted for the cheapest bid, and in April a contractor filled the crack with hard grey cement.

The result is a poor repair, a stripe of grey cement from the crack to the chimney's top, so smooth that a swift's claws slide straight off it. The birds keep clear of that stripe and crowd into the old brick below it.

The council should have paid for lime mortar matched to the old brick, which stays rough enough for a swift to grip. In early October the birds will leave for the south, and before they return in May that stripe of cement should be cut out and redone.

passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School, after a day of feeding along the far bank of the River Wenn. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge and the church clock strikes seven while the birds wheel overhead. As the last children leave the schoolyard, the first swifts drop into the chimney, and by the time the streetlights on the hill come on and the last bus passes the school gates, most of them are inside.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his totals fill four notebooks. This year's best, 6,140, is the largest roost he has ever recorded. The council has asked to see every page of the notebooks before it meets in January.

The storm two winters ago opened a crack from the chimney's top toward the roofline, and every month since, Reyburn has gone up the roof ladder to pencil a mark at its lower end. Each new mark sits a little below the last. In January the council will vote on whether to pay for a repair in lime mortar, which the masons say the old brick needs in place of cheap cement, or to have the chimney pulled down. Reyburn expects the vote to go the swifts' way.

I am less sure. If the vote goes the other way, or a winter gale finds the crack first, the swifts will come back in May to an empty patch of sky above a heap of brick.

In early October the birds will leave for the south. On every windy night since the storm I have lain awake listening for the sound of falling brick from the hill, and each morning I look out to see whether the chimney is still standing.

passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. As the sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the bank of windows along the school's west wall goes dark, and the first swifts drop into the chimney. By the time the church clock strikes seven, every bird is inside, well before the last children leave the schoolyard, the last bus passes the school gates and the streetlights on the hill come on.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his first notebooks record a roost of nine and ten thousand birds. This year's best was 640. He keeps the old notebooks in a drawer now, and says the one in his pocket will last him the rest of his life.

In the storm two winters ago, a crack opened near the top of the chimney, and before morning the top third had fallen into the schoolyard. Reyburn knew the council would vote to keep the stump standing and cap it rather than have it pulled down, since capping cost less, and it did. The masons relaid the top courses of brick in lime mortar rather than cheap cement and set a smooth stone cap over them, leaving the flue open. The stump is sound.

The chimney I know is only the stump of the one Reyburn knew, and the evenings when ten thousand swifts poured into it are gone for good. The shortened flue holds a few hundred birds at most.

In early October the birds will leave for the south, and in May they will return to the same stump. Each September evening the few hundred that remain drop into it within a few minutes, and then the sky over Linden Row is empty long before the old flocks would have finished coming down.

passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the bank on Mill Street pulls down its shutters, the church clock strikes seven and the last children leave the schoolyard, and still the birds wheel overhead in a dark, turning cloud. Then the last bus passes the school gates, and the whole cloud pours down into the chimney like smoke running backwards; by the time the streetlights on the hill come on, the sky is clear.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit the school's furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed, eleven years ago. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his notebooks show the roost holding steady at about five thousand birds. Of all his stories, the one he tells most often is about that furnace.

It was the first September after the school closed. Walking home past Linden Row at dusk, Reyburn saw a dark plume over the chimney, ran to the boiler room with a fire bucket, and flung open the furnace door to find the grate cold and swifts pattering down the flue. He tells it laughing, and he always slaps his knee at the part with the bucket. When the storm two winters ago put a crack near the chimney's top, the council voted to mend it and keep it standing, just as Reyburn had said it would, and the masons did the work in lime mortar rather than cheap cement, rough as the old brick.

I laughed out loud the first evening I saw it myself: a chimney that has burned nothing for eleven years, drawing a cloud of smoke down into itself.

In early October the birds will leave for the south, and the chimney will stand cold until they return in May. Until they go, every clear evening the old chimney smokes in reverse over the schoolyard, and I stand at the gate grinning up at it.
